paragraphs.source_en: In this chronological-stylistic sequence of the Saharan rock art, domesticated cattle dominate the carved or painted compositions. However, engravings of this style are controversial in that their technique and patina are often very similar to the Bubaline engravings. Indeed, some scholars (Muzzolini 1995a, b; Jelinek 2004; Le Quellec 2006b) believe that these two phases or styles are in reality only one single artistic tradition and they propose to place both of them in the Neolithic period.

paragraphs.source_en: Regarding the Pastoral paintings, they are obviously distinguishable from the Round Heads (Fig. 2-5). The technique is different, using a tiny border of light red ochre, encircling figures which may or may not be filled with a similar red colour. In general, the figures are much smaller (usually no more than about 20 cm in height) and they are represented in great detail, including facial and anatomical features, which are never expressed in the Round Head art. The compositions are also different, with the abundance of everyday life scenes, the disappearance of masks, horns and other bodily attributes so frequent in the previous artistic tradition. It would not be wise to claim that the Pastoral art is purely secular and narrative; however, if it does represent an ideology or a religion, it is represented in a completely different fashion from the Round Head style.

paragraphs.source_en: Representations of domesticated cattle constitute the favourite theme of the painters. Hundreds of bulls and cows are represented in herds, although occasionally alone, and accompanied by images of men, who are painted with great attention to detail, showing correct anatomical proportions. The Pastoral paintings bear witness to a realistic conception of art which is far removed from the figurative symbolism featured by the Round Heads. This clear break in the pictures has been attributed to the arrival of new people in the Central Sahara.

paragraphs.source_en: Pastoral art is attested all over the Central Sahara which is likely to be related to the herdsmen lifestyle, which requires regular movement throughout a large territory in search of fresh pastures. In the area of the Round Head paintings images of domesticated cattle were sometimes added on the same walls but they are also found in new shelters without previous paintings, i. e. in those places which were not of interest for painters of the Round Head art.
